response.narrative: The run now has four large, internally robust, and externally within-dataset validated associations: TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency. The next scientific priority is not more validation of those accepted effects, but specificity, context, and broad exploration of previously under-tested outcomes. I therefore defer many small pending refinements, including the EGFR amplification strata and residual accepted-effect subgroup checks, because their existing point estimates are far below the clinically meaningful benchmark or the main effects are already accepted with supporting strata. I closed main broad oncogene nulls H1, H2, and H4 because the central questions have been answered in this dataset. The new hypotheses are designed as falsifiable specificity controls. H77 asks whether TP53 loss also weakens NFE2L2 dependency in the same way KEAP1 loss does; H78 asks whether KEAP1 loss also weakens USP7 dependency in the way TP53 loss does. Large cross-biomarker effects would suggest that the accepted reversal associations are not outcome- or pathway-specific and could reflect broader co-mutational or assay structure, whereas near-null results would strengthen the claim that TP53 loss specifically predicts USP7 dependency and KEAP1 loss specifically predicts NFE2L2 dependency. H79 extends the strong SMARCA4-loss effect to the previously under-tested TMED10 outcome; a large effect would raise concern about broader BAF-related or screen-wide dependency structure, while a null result supports TMED10 specificity and leaves SMARCA2 as the main BAF paralog-associated outcome. H80 tests CDKN2A loss versus MDM2 dependency. CDKN2A loss is a plausible p53-pathway predictor independent of direct TP53 loss, and a clinically meaningful negative raw difference, reflected here as a positive signed estimate under direction -1, would identify a new MDM2 dependency marker. I keep H68 and H76 active as complementary POLR2A specificity controls, H69 and H70 as KRAS-wild-type context checks for the reversal effects, H42 and H47 as marker-E specificity controls, H22 as the existing TMED10 marker control, and H72 as an RAS-pathway exploration of NF1 loss versus RIT1 dependency. All interpretations remain dataset-specific associations, not causal claims or generalizable biological claims.

response.narrative: I select twelve analyses aimed mainly at specificity and broad untested associations rather than additional validation of the four accepted large effects. First, H77 and H78 are cross-biomarker controls: TP53 loss on NFE2L2 dependency and KEAP1 loss on USP7 dependency. Large effects would challenge the outcome specificity of the accepted TP53-USP7 and KEAP1-NFE2L2 associations, while near-null results would strengthen the interpretation that these are selective associations rather than broad consequences of correlated pathway alterations. Second, H79, H68, and H76 are cross-outcome controls on under-tested dependencies: SMARCA4 loss versus TMED10 dependency, SMARCA4 loss versus POLR2A dependency, and MSI-high versus POLR2A dependency. Near-null estimates would support that the SMARCA2 and WRN effects are not generic shifts in broad essential dependency or screen structure, whereas large effects would warrant confounding investigations. Third, H42, H47, H74, and H75 complete role-free marker controls for USP7 and NFE2L2 using markers E and F, complementing the null marker-D controls. This tests whether the accepted large reversal effects are tied to assay-agnostic markers. Fourth, H80 tests CDKN2A loss versus MDM2 dependency, a plausible p53-pathway predictor independent of direct TP53 loss. Finally, H72 and H73 test NF1 loss versus RIT1 and KRAS dependency, respectively, because NF1 loss activates RAS/MAPK signaling and provides a pathway-level follow-up after direct KRAS mutation was not associated with KRAS dependency. I defer EGFR refinements and KRAS-wild-type context checks for accepted effects this round because EGFR estimates are small and the accepted effects already have strong validation and multiple stratum controls.

response.narrative:
The new specificity controls are largely reassuring for the four accepted large associations. H77 tests whether TP53 loss also predicts weaker NFE2L2 dependency in the same way KEAP1 loss does: R54 = +0.016 [-0.025, 0.056] under a positive direction. The point estimate is small and imprecise, with no evidence of a clinically meaningful association. H78 tests whether KEAP1 loss also predicts weaker USP7 dependency: R55 = +0.009 [-0.033, 0.050], also near null. These cross-biomarker nulls support outcome specificity: TP53 loss is associated with USP7 dependency in this dataset, and KEAP1 loss is associated with NFE2L2 dependency, but neither appears to produce the opposite very large cross-outcome effect. This does not exclude small associations, but it argues against the accepted effects being generic manifestations of broad pathway co-alteration.

The cross-outcome controls are also reassuring. SMARCA4 loss is not meaningfully associated with TMED10 dependency, R56 = -0.005 [-0.025, 0.014], or POLR2A dependency, R57 = -0.005 [-0.024, 0.014]. MSI-high is not meaningfully associated with POLR2A dependency, R58 = -0.004 [-0.035, 0.028]. Because the accepted SMARCA2 and WRN effects are enormous, a generic shift in broad essential dependency or screen-wide quality would plausibly have produced large effects on TMED10 or POLR2A as well. The near-null results therefore support that the SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 and MSI-high/WRN associations are relatively selective in this dataset.

Role-free marker controls are consistent with specificity. Marker-E is not associated with USP7 or NFE2L2 dependency: R60 = -0.008 [-0.040, 0.025] and R61 = +0.001 [-0.031, 0.033]. Marker-F is also near null for USP7 and NFE2L2: R62 = -0.024 [-0.056, 0.009] and R63 = -0.006 [-0.038, 0.026]. These are far smaller than the accepted large biomarker effects and do not support the idea that assay-agnostic marker structure is driving the main findings. I reject and close these marker-control claims.

The NF1-loss RAS-pathway explorations are null in the claimed direction. NF1 loss is not associated with stronger RIT1 dependency, R64 = -0.021 [-0.049, 0.008], nor stronger KRAS dependency, R65 = -0.020 [-0.049, 0.009]. These are small and imprecise, and do not support a clinically meaningful dependency-marker association in this dataset. I reject and close them.

The only new non-null discovery is H80, CDKN2A loss versus MDM2 dependency. Because H80 has direction -1, the signed estimate R59 = +0.117 [0.082, 0.152] corresponds to a negative raw exposed-minus-comparator difference: CDKN2A-loss tumors have more negative MDM2 scores, i.e. stronger MDM2 dependency. The effect is not huge relative to the previously validated associations, which are around +0.8, but it is moderate, precise, and clinically meaningful by the stated threshold: it is about 0.52 standard deviations of MDM2 dependency and its interval excludes very small EGFR-like effects. The direct TP53-loss association with MDM2 was null, so CDKN2A loss may identify a p53-pathway context for MDM2 dependency through a different mechanism, possibly involving cell-cycle or co-deletion structure. Given the large number of discovery comparisons tested, I do not want to close on discovery alone, but the evidence is strong enough to accept the dataset association now while validation is run. I therefore accept H80, keep it active, and request independent validation. If validation confirms, H80 can become an additional robust predictor of stronger MDM2 dependency in this dataset. If validation fails or is unstable, I will revisit its status.

All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal claims and not claims of external generalizability.

The new analysis block adds a fifth dataset-specific association: H80 CDKN2A loss -> stronger MDM2 dependency, R59 = +0.117 [0.082, 0.152] under direction -1. Specificity controls are near null: cross-biomarker H77 TP53/NFE2L2 and H78 KEAP1/USP7; cross-outcome H79 SMARCA4/TMED10, H68 SMARCA4/POLR2A, H76 MSI/POLR2A; marker-E/F controls H42 USP7/E, H47 NFE2L2/E, H74 USP7/F, H75 NFE2L2/F; NF1 exploratory tests H72 RIT1/NF1 and H73 KRAS/NF1. response.narrative:
The new validation evidence closes the last major open question about the four very large biomarker-dependency associations. For H6, MSI-high versus MSI-low or MSI-negative status in dependency_WRN, independent validation gives R53 = +0.821 [0.766, 0.877] at the stricter validation alpha = 0.00385, with valid cell sizes 125 and 1875. Because H6 has direction -1, this signed positive estimate corresponds to a strongly negative raw exposed-minus-comparator difference: MSI-high tumors have substantially more negative WRN dependency scores, i.e. stronger WRN dependency. This is concordant with, and slightly larger than, the discovery estimate R6 = +0.790 [0.760, 0.819]. The validated interval is very far from zero and the magnitude is far above the task's 10% clinically significant difference benchmark; relative to the observed WRN score standard deviation (~0.263), it is roughly a three-standard-deviation effect. Combined with prior internal robustness checks—Avana-library stratum R18 +0.813, batch_a main effect R41 +0.824, batch_b main effect R42 +0.789, high-mutation-burden stratum R43 +0.775, high-Cas9 stratum R44 +0.776, KRAS-wild-type context R45 +0.792, and null marker-D/E/F controls—this supports acceptance of MSI-high as a strong dataset-specific predictor of stronger WRN dependency. I close H6. This remains an association within the supplied dataset; it is not proof of causality or external generalizability. The only residual technical gap is the non-Avana WRN stratum, which could not be estimated because the exposed cell had only 10 observations in R27; however, the independent overall validation substantially mitigates the discovery-multiplicity concern.

The H17 response deadline is satisfied. KEAP1 loss versus no KEAP1 loss in dependency_NFE2L2 remains accepted: discovery R8 = +0.796 [0.776, 0.816] and validation R26 = +0.791 [0.761, 0.821]. Direction +1 means the raw exposed-minus-comparator difference is positive, so KEAP1-loss tumors have less negative NFE2L2 scores, i.e. weaker NFE2L2 dependency. This is a robust reversal of the initially hypothesized synthetic-lethal direction in H8, which remains rejected. I reaffirm H17 as accepted and closed.

The current supported large-association set is therefore: TP53 loss predicts much weaker USP7 dependency (H11 accepted and validated); KEAP1 loss predicts much weaker NFE2L2 dependency (H17 accepted and validated; H8 rejected); SMARCA4 loss predicts much stronger SMARCA2 dependency (H7 accepted and validated, with multiple stratum and specificity controls); and MSI-high predicts much stronger WRN dependency (H6 now accepted and validated). The SMARCA2 finding is further supported by Avana stratum validation H28, non-Avana discovery R28, ARID1A-wild-type stratum R35, TP53-wild-type stratum R51, and batch_a main effect R50. Role-free marker controls for these outcomes are near null, including marker-D, marker-E, and marker-F tests for WRN and SMARCA2, and marker-D for NFE2L2 and USP7.

The scientifically important negative findings remain dataset-specific and informative: direct matched oncogene-mutation or amplification associations were generally weak or null. KRAS mutation was not associated with stronger KRAS dependency; STK11 loss was not associated with KRAS dependency; BRAF V600E was not associated with BRAF dependency; ERBB2 amplification was not associated with ERBB2 dependency; TP53 loss was not associated with stronger MDM2 dependency; PIK3CA mutation was not associated with stronger STAT3 dependency; MYC amplification was not associated with stronger DHX9, RPL11, or POLR2A dependency; and BRCA2 loss was not associated with stronger KIF18A dependency. ARID1A loss overall was not associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, while SMARCA4 loss was strongly associated, supporting a more SMARCA4-specific paralogous dependence pattern rather than generic BAF-complex loss.

EGFR amplification remains the main unresolved candidate among the clinically motivated oncogene-dependency hypotheses. Several EGFR comparisons are directionally consistent with stronger EGFR dependency, including the overall estimate R3 +0.025 [-0.000, 0.051], KRAS-wild-type context R22 +0.016 [-0.014, 0.046], TP53-loss context R37 +0.025 [-0.031, 0.080], and driver-exclusive adenocarcinoma refinement R52 +0.021 [-0.017, 0.060]. However, these point estimates are small relative to the accepted huge associations and often underpowered. EGFR should not be accepted unless a more informative stratum or pooled refinement yields a clinically meaningful, reasonably precise effect and preferably independent validation. Other unresolved questions include whether the accepted large effects persist in additional co-mutational or assay-quality strata, especially TP53-loss/USP7 and KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 in KRAS-wild-type tumors, and whether cross-outcome specificity controls such as MSI-high/POLR2A and SMARCA4-loss/POLR2A are near null.

The most informative next analyses are therefore not further validation of the already validated large associations, but (1) completing specificity controls for the large effects, especially cross-outcome controls H76 MSI-high/POLR2A and H68 SMARCA4-loss/POLR2A, plus remaining marker-E/F controls for USP7 and NFE2L2; (2) testing whether the large reversal effects remain in co-mutational contexts H69 TP53-loss/USP7 in KRAS-wild-type tumors and H70 KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 in KRAS-wild-type tumors; and (3) resolving EGFR with the registered co-mutation-stratum refinements H14, H38, H48, and related EGFR hypotheses rather than validating the weak overall EGFR signal. These analyses will better distinguish biomarker-specific associations from broader co-mutational structure, technical confounding, or underpowered small effects.

response.narrative:
No assessments are due, so I register new scientifically motivated comparisons while preserving existing unresolved robustness checks. The prior run established three very large dataset associations, but most other measured predictors remain either small or untested. I therefore add targeted biology and robustness questions.

First, I test MDM2 dependency through the p14ARF/MTAP/CDKN2A axis restricted to TP53-intact cells. CDKN2A encodes p14ARF, which inhibits MDM2; loss of CDKN2A could increase MDM2 pathway activity and therefore stronger MDM2 dependency, represented by a more negative dependency_MDM2 score. I register CDKN2A-loss versus CDKN2A-intact and MTAP-loss versus MTAP-intact in TP53-intact cells, both expected negative. MTAP is frequently co-deleted near CDKN2A and can proxy similar p14ARF/CDKN2A locus biology, so concordance would support a coherent axis; a large CDKN2A-only effect would favor CDKN2A-specific structure.

Second, I test more biologically selected RAS-pathway and RTK hypotheses. Direct KRAS-mutant versus wild-type effects were tiny, so I ask whether NF1 loss in KRAS-wild-type cells predicts stronger KRAS dependency. NF1 loss activates RAS signaling, and in the absence of KRAS mutation this may reveal dependency on endogenous KRAS signaling. I also test ERBB2 amplification among KRAS-wild-type cells because KRAS mutation can bypass EGFR/ERBB2 dependence; an association in KRAS-wild-type cells would be more informative for RTK dependency than an unselected analysis.

Third, I refine MYC hypotheses. Amplification alone may be too blunt, so I restrict MYC-amplification effects to cells above a high MYC-expression threshold. DHX9, USP7, POLR2A, and RPL11 are plausible MYC-associated vulnerabilities involving replication stress, protein stability, transcription, and translation. If MYC amplification is a biologically meaningful driver state only when accompanied by high MYC expression, these expression-restricted effects may be larger than the near-null amplification-only effects. If they remain small, MYC amplification is unlikely to be a strong predictor of these dependencies in this dataset.

Fourth, I add specificity and robustness checks for the accepted KEAP1/NFE2L2 signal. The prior STK11 co-loss interaction was near null, but a main effect restricted to STK11-intact cells can test whether the large positive effect is an artifact of KEAP1-STK11 co-deletion. I register KEAP1 loss versus KEAP1 intact among STK11-intact cells, with the registered positive direction matching the accepted weaker-NFE2L2-dependency association.

Finally, I test screen-quality moderation using screen_roc_auc median split. For accepted SMARCA2 and WRN effects, a near-null interaction would support stability; a more negative interaction would suggest stronger associations in higher-quality screens. For the KEAP1/NFE2L2 positive association, I use positive interaction direction for the same logic. These are dataset-level robustness checks, not external-validity claims.

I prioritize comparisons with adequate expected cell counts and avoid structurally impossible strata. Large, precise main effects would motivate later validation; near-zero MYC or screen-quality interactions would mainly narrow the space of additional predictors and support robustness of the accepted associations. All claims remain associations within this supplied dataset, not causal or generalizable findings.

No assessments are due, so I use the analysis slot to test the twelve newly registered high-specificity hypotheses rather than repeating already-tested comparisons. H99 and H100 test MDM2 dependency through p14ARF/CDKN2A and MTAP biology specifically in TP53-intact cells, where p53 pathway activity can make MDM2 dependency biologically interpretable. H101 tests whether NF1 loss in KRAS-wildtype cells predicts stronger KRAS dependency, a more biologically selected test than the weak overall KRAS-mutant contrast already observed. H102 tests ERBB2 amplification in KRAS-wildtype cells, where RTK dependence is less likely to be masked by KRAS-mutant bypass signaling. H103-H106 test MYC-amplification effects restricted to high MYC expression for DHX9, USP7, POLR2A, and RPL11, refining the near-null amplification-only MYC hypotheses. H107 tests the KEAP1/NFE2L2 association in STK11-intact cells to assess whether the large accepted effect is robust to KEAP1-STK11 co-deletion structure. Finally, H108-H110 test screen-quality moderation for the three accepted large associations using screen_roc_auc median split; near-null interactions would support robustness, while directionally large interactions would indicate dependence on screen quality. These analyses remain dataset-specific associations and not causal claims.

This wave provides strong robustness evidence for the three accepted large associations and completes the constructed-marker negative-control suite. Marker-E main effects are all close to zero for SMARCA2, WRN, and NFE2L2 (H34/H35/H36). Combined with the earlier marker-D and marker-F null controls, these results make it less plausible that the very large accepted signals are artifacts of the arbitrary constructed-marker encoding or marker-correlated structure; I therefore reject the marker-E association claims and close them. Library-restricted main effects are highly concordant with the overall effects. SMARCA4 loss predicts much stronger SMARCA2 dependency in both the dominant Avana library and the KY library, and MSI-high predicts much stronger WRN dependency in Avana. KEAP1 loss again predicts weaker NFE2L2 dependency in both Avana and KY. These library-specific effects are large and precise, so I accept H73-H77 as context-specific dataset associations and close them. Moderation tests are less supportive of an important effect-size interaction. The growth-rate interaction for SMARCA4/SMARCA2 (H80) is statistically marginal but opposite to the registered negative direction; raw interaction is small and positive, not practically meaningful compared with the main effect near -0.8, so I reject H80 rather than promoting an opposite small interaction. The growth-rate interaction for MSI-high/WRN (H81) is imprecise and does not support the registered negative direction. The mutation-burden interaction for MSI-high/WRN (H84) is invalid because the low-burden complement contains no MSI-high cells; this indicates structural overlap between MSI status and mutation burden in this dataset rather than a meaningful null interaction. The STK11 co-loss interaction for KEAP1/NFE2L2 (H92) is near null and does not support direction-specific moderation. I request independent validation for H26, the TP53-loss-specific KEAP1/NFE2L2 association, because it is an accepted large context effect not yet independently validated and validating it would complete the KEAP1/NFE2L2 assessment across both TP53 strata.
response.research_notes: Robustness update: marker-D, marker-E, and marker-F main effects are near null for SMARCA2, WRN, and NFE2L2; arbitrary constructed markers appear to be negative controls in this dataset. Accepted large associations now have extensive context consistency: SMARCA4 loss -> stronger SMARCA2 dependency overall and in Avana/KY, adenocarcinoma, ARID1A-intact cells; MSI-high -> stronger WRN dependency overall, Avana, adenocarcinoma, adherent culture; KEAP1 loss -> weaker NFE2L2 dependency overall, Avana/KY, TP53-intact and TP53-loss strata. Pending independent validation requested for H26 TP53-loss KEAP1/NFE2L2. Moderation: growth-rate interactions are small and do not support accepted direction; H80 raw interaction is weakly opposite but too small and likely not meaningful. MSI/WRN mutation-burden interaction H84 is invalid because all MSI-high cells appear above median mutation burden; do not revisit this contrast. STK11 co-loss interaction is near null. Remaining planned stress tests: media-serum main effects and interactions, ploidy interactions, culture-adherence interaction for KEAP1, marker-E interactions, growth-rate interaction for KEAP1/NFE2L2, and broader driver/MYC hypotheses. All conclusions remain associations within this supplied dataset only, not causal or generalizable claims.

response.narrative: The new validation evidence confirms both due claims and strengthens the core set of supported dataset-specific associations. For H7, SMARCA4 loss versus SMARCA4 intact in dependency_SMARCA2, the independent validation R26 is signed positive for the registered negative-direction claim: estimate +0.8006 with an independent interval [0.7713, 0.8300]. Because estimates are already signed to the hypothesis direction, the raw interpretation is that SMARCA4-loss lines have much more negative dependency_SMARCA2 scores than SMARCA4-intact lines, i.e. much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. Discovery R7 and validation R26 are highly concordant in magnitude and direction, so H7 remains accepted and closed. For H26, KEAP1 loss versus KEAP1 intact in dependency_NFE2L2 within TP53-loss cells, validation R53 is signed positive for the registered positive-direction claim: estimate +0.8046 with an independent interval [0.7383, 0.8708]. The raw interpretation is that TP53-loss KEAP1-loss cells have less negative dependency_NFE2L2 scores than TP53-loss KEAP1-intact cells, i.e. weaker NFE2L2 dependency. This is consistent with discovery R25 and with the independently validated TP53-intact conditional claim H20, where R40 estimated a very similar effect. Thus the KEAP1/NFE2L2 association is large in both TP53 strata and is independently validated for the TP53-loss stratum. Overall, the strongest evidence now supports three large associations in this supplied dataset: SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high status with much stronger WRN dependency, and KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency. The latter has been validated both overall as a reversed claim H19 and in TP53-intact H20 and TP53-loss H26 strata.
